items.stem: Which species is amphiprotic?
items.answer: HCO₃⁻
items.markingKey: A. Can donate or accept H⁺.

items.stem: Why does the conjugate base of a strong acid have negligible basic strength?
options: The acid fully donates its proton, so the conjugate base has almost no tendency to accept one back.
items.answer: The acid fully donates its proton, so the conjugate base has almost no tendency to accept one back.
items.markingKey: B. Inverse strength relationship.

items.stem: Explain the difference between an acid and its conjugate base.
items.answer: The conjugate base has one fewer H⁺ (and a charge one unit more negative) than the acid.
items.markingKey: The conjugate base has one fewer H⁺ (and a charge one unit more negative) than the acid. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Which species acts as a Brønsted–Lowry acid in the forward reaction HCO₃⁻ + PO₄³⁻ ⇌ CO₃²⁻ + HPO₄²⁻?
items.answer: HCO₃⁻
items.markingKey: D. HCO₃⁻ donates a proton to PO₄³⁻.

volume NaOH / cm³ | pH

7.50 | 2.39

items.answer: (a) 30.00 cm³ – the centre of the steepest rise in pH (b) pKa = pH at half-equivalence = 2.87 (c) The salt formed contains the conjugate base CH₂ClCOO⁻, which accepts protons from water forming OH⁻. items.stem: Hydrogencarbonate ions are important in blood. (a) Write equations to show that HCO₃⁻ is amphiprotic. (b) Identify the conjugate pairs in each equation. (c) Explain how HCO₃⁻ helps to keep blood pH roughly constant when acid enters the blood. (d) State the conjugate base of H₂CO₃ and of HCO₃⁻.
items.answer: (a) HCO₃⁻ + H₂O ⇌ CO₃²⁻ + H₃O⁺; HCO₃⁻ + H₃O⁺ ⇌ H₂CO₃ + H₂O. (b) HCO₃⁻/CO₃²⁻ & H₃O⁺/H₂O; H₃O⁺/H₂O & H₂CO₃/HCO₃⁻. (c) HCO₃⁻ accepts H⁺ to form H₂CO₃ (→ CO₂ + H₂O, exhaled), removing added acid. (d) HCO₃⁻; CO₃²⁻.
items.markingKey: (a) HCO₃⁻ + H₂O ⇌ CO₃²⁻ + H₃O⁺; HCO₃⁻ + H₃O⁺ ⇌ H₂CO₃ + H₂O. (b) HCO₃⁻/CO₃²⁻ & H₃O⁺/H₂O; H₃O⁺/H₂O & H₂CO₃/HCO₃⁻. (c) HCO₃⁻ accepts H⁺ to form H₂CO₃ (→ CO₂ + H₂O, exhaled), removing added acid. (d) HCO₃⁻; CO₃²⁻.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "oxonium ion"?
options: The H₃O⁺ ion, formed when a proton bonds to a water molecule
The point in a titration at which stoichiometrically equivalent amounts of acid and base have reacted
The point in a titration at which the indicator changes colour
The negative logarithm to base 10 of the hydrogen ion concentration: pH = −log₁₀[H⁺]
items.answer: The H₃O⁺ ion, formed when a proton bonds to a water molecule
items.markingKey: A. "oxonium ion" is the H₃O⁺ ion, formed when a proton bonds to a water molecule.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "conjugate acid–base pair".
items.answer: Two species that differ by one proton, e.g. NH₄⁺/NH₃
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: two species that differ by one proton, e.g. NH₄⁺/NH₃. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Priya writes: "A base must contain hydroxide ions." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: A Brønsted–Lowry base is any proton acceptor, e.g. NH₃, CO₃²⁻ or CH₃NH₂.
items.markingKey: A Brønsted–Lowry base is any proton acceptor, e.g. NH₃, CO₃²⁻ or CH₃NH₂. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain why H₃O⁺ is used to represent H⁺ in aqueous solution.
items.answer: A bare proton cannot exist alone in water; it bonds to a lone pair on a water molecule, forming the oxonium ion.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: A bare proton cannot exist alone in water; it bonds to a lone pair on a water molecule, forming the oxonium ion. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between a Brønsted–Lowry base and a Brønsted–Lowry acid.
items.answer: An acid donates a proton; a base accepts a proton using a lone pair.
items.markingKey: An acid donates a proton; a base accepts a proton using a lone pair. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Which pair is NOT a conjugate acid–base pair?
items.answer: H₃O⁺ and OH⁻
items.markingKey: B. Differ by two protons.

items.stem: For H₃O⁺ + F⁻ ⇌ H₂O + HF, state the two conjugate acid–base pairs.
items.answer: acids: H₃O⁺ and HF; bases: F⁻ and H₂O; pairs H₃O⁺/H₂O, HF/F⁻
items.markingKey: H₃O⁺/H₂O (1); HF/F⁻ (1).

items.stem: Which of CO₃²⁻, H₂O, NH₄⁺ and SO₄²⁻ is amphiprotic?
items.answer: H₂O
items.markingKey: D. H₂O can both donate a proton (→ OH⁻) and accept one (→ H₃O⁺).

items.stem: What is the conjugate acid of PO₄³⁻?
items.answer: HPO₄²⁻
items.markingKey: A. Add one H⁺ to PO₄³⁻: HPO₄²⁻.

items.stem: Write equations to show HSO₄⁻ acting as an acid with water and as a base with H₃O⁺.
items.answer: HSO₄⁻ + H₂O ⇌ SO₄²⁻ + H₃O⁺; HSO₄⁻ + H₃O⁺ ⇌ H₂SO₄ + H₂O
items.markingKey: HSO₄⁻ + H₂O ⇌ SO₄²⁻ + H₃O⁺; HSO₄⁻ + H₃O⁺ ⇌ H₂SO₄ + H₂O

items.stem: "Water is the most important amphiprotic substance in chemistry." Discuss.
items.answer: Water is uniquely important as the solvent, but other amphiprotic species are equally important in specific systems.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: solvent for most acid–base reactions; autoionisation sets the pH scale; acts as acid or base depending on partner. Arguments against: many other amphiprotic species are biologically vital (HCO₃⁻ buffer, H₂PO₄⁻, amino acids); non-aqueous solvents also show proton transfer. Supported judgement: Water is uniquely important as the solvent, but other amphiprotic species are equally important in specific systems. items.answer: ionic product of water (Kw)

items.stem: Explain why a tenfold dilution of a strong acid raises the pH by one unit.
items.answer: The strong acid is fully dissociated, so [H⁺] falls by a factor of 10, and −log of a value ten times smaller is one unit greater.

items.stem: "Measuring pH with a meter is always better than using universal indicator." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: A calibrated meter is far more precise, but indicator is acceptable when a rough value is enough.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: meters are precise (±0.01) and objective; can log data continuously. A solution in which [H⁺] = [OH⁻]; pH 7.00 only at 298 K
The reaction between an acid and a base to form a salt and water (H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O)
A graph of pH against the volume of titrant added during an acid–base titration
items.answer: The negative logarithm of the hydroxide ion concentration; pH + pOH = 14.00 at 298 K

items.stem: Explain the difference between pH and pOH.
items.answer: pH = −log[H⁺]; pOH = −log[OH⁻]; at 298 K they add up to 14.00.

items.stem: A student claims: "A solution of pH 2 is twice as acidic as a solution of pH 4." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: pH is logarithmic: pH 2 has [H⁺] 100 times greater than pH 4.
items.markingKey: pH is logarithmic: pH 2 has [H⁺] 100 times greater than pH 4. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between an acidic solution and a neutral solution.
items.answer: In an acidic solution [H⁺] > [OH⁻]; in a neutral solution they are equal (pH 7.00 only at 298 K).

Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "The pH scale is an adequate measure of acidity for all purposes."
items.answer: pH is ideal for everyday aqueous measurements but must be supplemented by concentration, pKa and buffer capacity.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: simple, widely understood, easily measured with meters and indicators; compresses a huge range. Arguments against: pH is temperature dependent (neutral point varies); does not distinguish strong/weak acids or show acid amount (buffering capacity); breaks down for very concentrated acids (negative pH). Supported judgement: pH is ideal for everyday aqueous measurements but must be supplemented by concentration, pKa and buffer capacity.
